subtopics.title: EOS-05 (GISAT-1A) and the GSLV-F17 launch
subtopics.summary: ISRO launched Earth Observation Satellite-05 (EOS-05), also called GISAT-1A, aboard GSLV-F17 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota. The booklet calls it India's first dedicated imaging satellite, designed to operate from a sub-geosynchronous orbit about 35,786 km above Earth. The launch was the 19th operational flight of GSLV and was described as validating India's cryogenic upper-stage technology for future human spaceflight.
facts: Launch vehicle: GSLV-F17, marked as the 19th operational flight of GSLV
Launch site: Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota
EOS-05 is India's first dedicated imaging satellite for sub-geosynchronous operations
Mass of EOS-05: approx 2,367 kg
Heaviest payload successfully injected into orbit by a GSLV
GSLV three stages: solid core first stage with 4 liquid strap-on boosters
GSLV second stage: liquid propellant
GSLV third stage: cryogenic
Nickname of EOS-05: 'Eye in the Sky'
EOS-05 carries optical and infrared imaging payloads

subtopics.title: Satellite orbits: LEO, MEO and GEO
subtopics.summary: An orbit is the curved path a satellite follows around Earth under gravity, and the choice of orbit shapes coverage, resolution, revisit time, delay and fuel need. LEO lies about 160-2,000 km up and offers low latency and high-resolution observation. MEO spans about 2,000-35,786 km and hosts navigation systems, while GEO is a special case of geosynchronous orbit at about 35,786 km.
facts: Orbit: curved path followed by a satellite around Earth under gravity
Orbit choice determines coverage, image resolution, revisit time, delay, fuel and mission
LEO altitude: approx 160-2,000 km; orbital period about 90-120 minutes
LEO features: low communication latency, suited to large constellations
Sun-synchronous orbit: LEO subtype giving relatively consistent solar illumination
Very Low Earth Orbit: very high-resolution observation but greater atmospheric drag
MEO altitude: approx 2,000 km to 35,786 km
MEO use: navigation systems such as GPS and Europe's Galileo
Geosynchronous orbit period equals Earth's rotation (23 hrs, 56 mins, 4 secs)
GEO: zero-degree inclination, directly over the Equator, moving in Earth's rotation direction
A GEO satellite appears fixed over one point on Earth

subtopics.title: Why GEO imaging matters and its uses
subtopics.summary: A LEO satellite observes a location only when it passes overhead, which leaves intervals between observations. A geosynchronous imaging platform can give persistent, wide-area monitoring, useful for fast events such as cyclones, cloudbursts, flash floods and forest fires. The booklet lists EOS-05 applications under disaster management, strategic and national security, and agriculture and environment.
facts: LEO satellite sees a particular location only when it passes overhead
Geosynchronous platform provides persistent and wide-area monitoring
Useful for tracking cyclones, cloudbursts, flash floods and forest fires
Frequent observations support weather monitoring, disaster management, early warning and emergency response
Disaster management: near real-time monitoring of cyclones, floods and cloudbursts
Strategic security: continuous surveillance of land borders and maritime domain
Agriculture and environment: monitoring forest fires, vegetation health and crop cycles
Optical sensors cannot penetrate thick clouds
High altitude limits sub-meter spatial resolution
Crop insurance claims streamlined by replacing manual experiments with objective satellite indices

subtopics.title: NISAR: NASA-ISRO radar satellite
subtopics.summary: NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) is described as the first joint Earth-observation satellite of NASA and ISRO. As a radar satellite it uses microwave pulses to capture sharp images in darkness and through clouds, unlike cameras that rely on visible light. Its data supports study of solid Earth processes, natural hazards, biomass and crop health.
facts: First joint Earth-observation satellite by NASA and ISRO
Uses microwave pulses, so it works in darkness and through clouds
World's first radar satellite using dual S- and L-band frequencies
Designed for a 3-year mission life
Orbit: 747 km, Sun-Synchronous (Low Earth) Orbit with a 12-day repeat cycle
The NASA-side radar, with a wavelength of about 24 cm, was developed by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)
Sweep SAR captures wide 3D high-resolution images over a 242 km swath
Large 12-metre antenna for receiving signals
Detects minute ground shifts for tectonic and structural analysis
Tracks biomass, deforestation, crop health and soil moisture; assesses earthquakes, floods, landslides and volcanoes

quizzes.passage:
An orbit is the curved path that a satellite follows around Earth under the influence of gravity. Mission designers must weigh several trade-offs before they choose one, and no single orbit suits every purpose. Earth orbits are classified by altitude, by inclination and by shape. Shape refers to whether an orbit is circular or elliptical, and inclination refers to its tilt relative to the Equator.

Satellites are commonly grouped into three broad families. The first family is Low Earth Orbit, the closest of the three to the planet. Its satellites are widely used for Earth observation and communication, and crewed platforms such as the International Space Station also operate in this zone. Several sub-types exist for particular purposes, including the Sun-synchronous orbit and the Very Low Earth Orbit. Both of these are sub-types of Low Earth Orbit.

The second family is Medium Earth Orbit. Mission planners place it beyond the first family but below the third. The third family is Geosynchronous Orbit, and Geostationary Orbit is a special case within it. Geostationary Orbit is used for communication, weather and imaging. Each family is described in order of increasing distance from Earth, and each differs in altitude, latency and typical use.

quizzes.passage:
An orbit is the curved path a satellite follows around Earth under the influence of gravity. Different orbits suit different missions, and the orbit a satellite uses determines the kind of work it can do. Earth orbits are classified by altitude, by inclination and by shape. Inclination is the tilt of an orbit relative to the Equator, and shape refers to whether an orbit is circular or elliptical. Some families lie close to the planet, while others lie far above it. Navigation systems also rely on satellites placed in one of these families.

The lowest family is often used for Earth observation and communication, and it suits large constellations of satellites. Low communication latency is a key feature of this family. Crewed space stations also operate in this closer region. Within the lowest family, specialised sub-types exist for particular purposes. Each family is linked to particular mission applications.

A middle family lies farther away than the lowest family. The highest family, known as geosynchronous, is defined by the timing of a satellite's revolution relative to the planet's spin. A special member of this family appears to hang above one place on the ground, which makes it useful for watching the same region continuously.

quizzes.passage:
ISRO launched Earth Observation Satellite 05, known as EOS-05, from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota. The satellite is also called GISAT-1A, and the booklet describes it as India's first dedicated imaging satellite. It is designed to operate from a sub-geosynchronous orbit.

The launch validated India's cryogenic upper-stage technology for future human spaceflight, according to the booklet. The booklet also says it is the heaviest payload a GSLV has injected into orbit. Its launch was the nineteenth operational flight of the GSLV.

A low orbit satellite sees a given location only when it passes overhead, which leaves gaps between observations. A satellite that stays over one region of the planet can instead keep a wide area under watch for long periods. The booklet lists a fixed, 24/7 footprint over the Indian subcontinent as a geostationary advantage. Such platforms are described as useful for tracking cyclones, cloudbursts, flash floods and forest fires.

EOS-05 is equipped with optical and infrared imaging payloads, and its applications are presented under three headings: disaster management, strategic and national security, and agriculture and environment. Each heading is linked to a set of monitoring tasks, and the booklet lists examples under each one. The booklet presents these points together in a short summary of the satellite and its applications.

quizzes.passage:
A satellite in a low orbit sees a given location only when it passes overhead, which leaves gaps between observations. A satellite that stays over one region of the planet can instead keep a wide area under watch for long periods.

The booklet connects this kind of monitoring with several tasks. Persistent watch can help track storms and floods, and it can support warnings issued before a hazard grows. Surveillance of the sea approaches and the land frontiers is also mentioned, as are checks on plant cover and forest condition. The booklet also says that the use of such data can streamline crop insurance claims.

EOS-05 is India's first dedicated imaging satellite and is also known by another name. It carries optical and infrared imaging payloads, and it is designed to operate from a sub-geosynchronous orbit. The satellite's optical sensors form one part of its imaging system, and the booklet also notes that the sensors face physical limits.

Another listed advantage is a steady footprint that stays fixed over the same land all day. Cyclones, cloudbursts and flash floods are among the events that the booklet mentions. The booklet presents these uses as part of the satellite's significance for India. Each use is described with a short list of examples.
